title: Introduction to Statistics: A Simulation-First Approach
text:
Welcome
This is an open educational resource (OER) for introductory statistics, built on a simulation-first pedagogy. Students develop statistical reasoning through hands-on simulation before encountering formal mathematical theory.

title: Introduction to Statistics: A Simulation-First Approach
text:
Why simulation first?
Traditional introductory statistics courses begin with probability rules and distribution theory, then use those tools to build confidence intervals and hypothesis tests. Students memorize formulas without understanding why they work.
This textbook reverses that order:

Explore data — See patterns, describe distributions, visualize relationships.
Simulate inference — Use resampling (bootstrap, permutation) to understand what inference is and why it works.
Approximate with theory — Learn that the normal and \(t\)-distributions are mathematical shortcuts for what simulation does directly.
Formalize probability — Study probability rules and random variables after students already have deep intuition about randomness.
Model relationships — Apply all inference tools to regression and categorical data.

By the time students encounter the Central Limit Theorem, they have already built sampling distributions hundreds of times. The theorem becomes an elegant confirmation of what they’ve seen, not an abstract declaration to accept on faith.

title: Introduction to Statistics: A Simulation-First Approach
text:
About this book
This textbook remixes material from two outstanding open-source statistics textbooks:

Introduction to Modern Statistics (2nd edition) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin
OpenIntro Statistics by David Diez, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Christopher Barr

Both are licensed under Creative Commons BY-SA 3.0, and this remix is shared under the same license.
Interactive simulations are powered by SimKit, an open-source statistics visualization toolkit developed at the University of Wisconsin-La Crosse.

title: 1  Preface
text:
For instructors
This textbook is designed around the simulation-based inference (SBI) approach popularized by Lock, Lock, Lock, Lock, and Lock in Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data. The pedagogical sequence is:
EDA → Simulation inference → Theoretical inference → Probability → Modeling
The book contains more material than most one-semester courses will cover. The 28 chapters are organized into eight parts, and instructors should select the chapters that fit their curriculum. A typical 15-week course might cover:
Parts IV.15–16,18 (advanced probability) and Part V (power/sample size) are included for courses that need them but can be omitted without loss of continuity.

title: 1  Preface
text:
SimKit integration
SimKit is a free, browser-based statistics toolkit that supports the simulation-first approach. The text features SimKit throughout but is written to be self-contained — instructors who prefer StatKey, R’s infer package, or other tools can substitute freely.
SimKit activities in this text use URL parameters for reproducibility. For example:
https://datascienceuwl.github.io/simkit/simulate/bootstrap-mean/?seed=42&n=30
The seed parameter ensures every student who uses the same link gets identical results, enabling graded simulation-based assignments.

title: 1  Preface
text:
Accessibility
This textbook is designed to meet WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility standards:

Text: Atkinson Hyperlegible font, designed for readers with low vision
Math: MathJax rendering with screen reader support
Color: All color choices meet 4.5:1 contrast ratio; information is never conveyed by color alone
Structure: Semantic HTML with proper heading hierarchy
Images: All figures include descriptive alt text
Navigation: Full keyboard accessibility with visible focus indicators

If you encounter accessibility barriers, please file an issue on the book’s GitHub repository.

title: Data and Exploration
text: Before we can draw conclusions from data, we need to understand what data is, where it comes from, and what it looks like. In Part I we develop the vocabulary and visual tools for exploring data — skills that form the foundation for everything that follows.

title: 2  Introduction to Data
text:
2.1 Case study: Using stents to prevent strokes
We start with a real example that illustrates both the power and the nuance of statistical analysis.
In a 2003 study, researchers investigated whether implanting a stent (a small mesh tube) in the brain of a patient at risk for a stroke would reduce the risk of a stroke.1
The researchers randomly assigned 451 at-risk patients to one of two groups:
The results at 30 days:
The treatment group had a higher stroke rate (14.7%) than the control group (5.7%). The stent appeared to increase the risk of stroke in the short term — the opposite of what researchers hoped.
This example highlights a key principle: a single study’s results can be surprising, and statistics gives us the tools to evaluate whether a result is real or could be due to random chance.

title: 2  Introduction to Data
text:
2.2 Observations, variables, and data frames
Every statistical analysis begins with data — a structured collection of information. Let’s establish the vocabulary.

An observation (also called a case or unit) is a single entity in a dataset. A variable is a characteristic that is measured or recorded for each observation. A data frame (or data table) organizes observations as rows and variables as columns.

Consider a dataset of students in an introductory statistics class. Each student is an observation. Variables might include:

Age (in years)
Major (e.g., Biology, Psychology, Undeclared)
GPA
Whether the student has taken a statistics course before (Yes/No)

title: 2  Introduction to Data
text:
2.3 Types of variables
Variables come in two fundamental types:

A numerical variable (or quantitative variable) takes on values that are numbers where arithmetic operations (like averaging) make sense. Examples: height, temperature, income, test score.
A categorical variable (or qualitative variable) takes on values that are labels or categories. Examples: eye color, zip code, political party, treatment group.

Numerical variables can be further classified:

Continuous: Can take any value in an interval (e.g., height = 172.4 cm)
Discrete: Can only take whole-number or countable values (e.g., number of siblings = 3)

Categorical variables can be further classified:

Nominal: Categories with no natural ordering (e.g., eye color: blue, brown, green)
Ordinal: Categories with a meaningful order (e.g., education level: high school, bachelor’s, graduate)


Zip codes are categorical, not numerical. Even though zip codes are written as numbers, it doesn’t make sense to compute the average zip code. The digits encode geography, not quantity. A good test: does it make sense to add, subtract, or average the values? If not, the variable is categorical.


Classify each variable as continuous numerical, discrete numerical, nominal categorical, or ordinal categorical:

Number of text messages sent per day
Favorite type of music
Temperature in Fahrenheit
Satisfaction rating (1 = very unsatisfied, …, 5 = very satisfied)

4

title: 2  Introduction to Data
text:
2.4 Relationships between variables
Statistics is often about understanding how variables relate to each other. We use specific terminology:

When we suspect that one variable might influence or predict another, we call the potential influencing variable the explanatory variable (or independent variable) and the variable being influenced the response variable (or dependent variable).

For example, in the stent study:

Explanatory variable: Treatment group (stent vs. control)
Response variable: Whether the patient had a stroke


Identifying one variable as “explanatory” does not necessarily mean it causes changes in the response. Establishing causation requires specific study designs (discussed in Chapter 2).

title: 2  Introduction to Data
text:
2.5 Chapter review

2.5.1 Summary

Statistics is the science of collecting, analyzing, and drawing conclusions from data.
A data frame organizes observations (rows) and variables (columns).
Variables are numerical (continuous or discrete) or categorical (nominal or ordinal).
Explanatory variables may predict or influence response variables.
Even well-designed studies can produce surprising results — statistical tools help us determine whether results are real or due to chance.

title: Simulation-Based Inference
text:
How can we draw conclusions about a population from a single sample? In Part II we answer this question through simulation. By resampling data thousands of times, we build an intuitive understanding of sampling variability, hypothesis testing, and confidence intervals — without formulas or distribution tables.
This is the heart of the simulation-first approach: understand the logic of inference before learning the mathematical shortcuts.

title: 9  Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
9.1 The big idea: resampling
Imagine you want to estimate the average height of all UW-La Crosse students. You take a random sample of 30 students and compute the sample mean: \(\bar{x} = 170.2\) cm.
How confident should you be that \(\bar{x} = 170.2\) is close to the true population mean \(\mu\)? If you took a different sample, you’d get a different \(\bar{x}\). But you can’t keep taking new samples from the population — you only have the one sample you collected.
The bootstrap idea: Treat your sample as a stand-in for the population and resample from it. Each bootstrap resample is drawn with replacement from your original sample, at the same sample size \(n\).
Why does this work? If the original sample is representative of the population, then resampling from it mimics what would happen if we could repeatedly sample from the population itself.

title: 9  Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text: A bootstrap resample is a sample of size \(n\) drawn with replacement from the original sample. The statistic computed from a bootstrap resample is called a bootstrap statistic. The collection of many bootstrap statistics forms the bootstrap distribution.

title: 9  Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
9.2 Bootstrapping in action
Let’s build a bootstrap confidence interval step by step.

9.2.1 Step 1: Collect data
Suppose we have a random sample of \(n = 30\) heights (in cm):
168, 172, 165, 180, 175, 162, 171, 169, 178, 173,
166, 170, 174, 167, 176, 163, 172, 169, 177, 171,
164, 173, 168, 175, 170, 166, 179, 172, 168, 174
The sample mean is \(\bar{x} = 171.2\) cm.


9.2.2 Step 2: Resample with replacement
We draw a new sample of 30 values from the original 30, with replacement. Some values will be repeated, others left out. For example, one bootstrap resample might be:
172, 172, 165, 175, 175, 162, 171, 171, 178, 173,
166, 170, 174, 172, 176, 163, 172, 169, 177, 171,
164, 173, 168, 175, 170, 166, 179, 172, 172, 174
This resample has a mean of \(\bar{x}^* = 171.5\) cm. The asterisk (\(*\)) denotes a bootstrap statistic.


9.2.3 Step 3: Repeat many times
We repeat Step 2 a large number of times — typically \(B = 1{,}000\) or more — and record the bootstrap mean each time. This gives us a bootstrap distribution of 1,000 means.


9.2.4 Step 4: Find the confidence interval
For a 95% confidence interval, we find the middle 95% of the bootstrap distribution by taking the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.

Try it yourself! Use SimKit to generate a bootstrap distribution and confidence interval:
Launch Bootstrap CI for One Sample

Paste the 30 heights above (or use SimKit’s built-in dataset).
Click +1000 to generate 1,000 bootstrap resamples.
Observe the bootstrap distribution forming.
Read the 95% confidence interval from the output.

How does the bootstrap distribution relate to the original sample mean?

title: 9  Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
9.3 Interpreting a confidence interval

A 95% confidence interval is a range of plausible values for the population parameter. We are 95% confident that the interval captures the true parameter value.


What “95% confident” means: If we repeated the entire study many times — collecting a new sample each time and computing a new 95% confidence interval — approximately 95% of those intervals would contain the true population parameter. Any single interval either contains the parameter or it doesn’t; the 95% refers to the long-run success rate of the procedure.


Common misinterpretation: “There is a 95% probability that the true mean is in this interval.” This statement treats the population mean as random and the interval as fixed. In fact, the population mean is fixed (we just don’t know it) and the interval is random (it depends on which sample we happened to collect).


A 95% bootstrap CI for the mean height of UW-La Crosse students is (167.8, 174.6). Which of the following interpretations is correct?

95% of all UW-La Crosse students have heights between 167.8 and 174.6 cm.
There is a 95% probability that the true mean height is between 167.8 and 174.6.
We are 95% confident that the true mean height of all UW-La Crosse students is between 167.8 and 174.6 cm.

1

title: 9  Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
9.4 The percentile method
The approach we’ve used is called the percentile method for bootstrap confidence intervals.

For a \((1 - \alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval using the percentile method:

Lower bound = the \((\alpha/2) \times 100\)th percentile of the bootstrap distribution
Upper bound = the \((1 - \alpha/2) \times 100\)th percentile of the bootstrap distribution

For a 95% CI (\(\alpha = 0.05\)): use the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. For a 90% CI (\(\alpha = 0.10\)): use the 5th and 95th percentiles. For a 99% CI (\(\alpha = 0.01\)): use the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles.


If you increase the confidence level from 95% to 99%, what happens to the width of the confidence interval? Why?2

title: 9  Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
section: 9.5 What affects the width of a CI?
text:
9.5 What affects the width of a CI?
Three factors control how wide a confidence interval is:

Sample size (\(n\)): Larger samples → narrower intervals (more information about the population)
Variability in the data: More spread → wider intervals (less precision)
Confidence level: Higher confidence → wider intervals (more certainty requires a wider net)


Explore it! Return to the Bootstrap CI tool and experiment:

Try different sample sizes. How does the CI width change?
Try 90% vs 95% vs 99% confidence levels. What happens?

title: 9  Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
9.6 Bootstrap CI for other statistics
The beauty of bootstrapping is its generality. The same resampling logic works for any statistic, not just the mean:

Median: Resample → compute median → repeat → percentile CI
Proportion: Resample → compute proportion → repeat → percentile CI
Standard deviation: Resample → compute SD → repeat → percentile CI
Difference in means: Resample from each group → compute difference → repeat → percentile CI

title: 9  Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
9.7 Chapter review

9.7.1 Summary

The bootstrap constructs a confidence interval by resampling with replacement from the original sample.
The bootstrap distribution approximates the sampling distribution of the statistic.
The percentile method uses the middle \((1 - \alpha) \times 100\%\) of the bootstrap distribution as the CI.
Bootstrap CIs work for any statistic — means, medians, proportions, differences, and more.
CI width depends on sample size, data variability, and confidence level.
“95% confident” means the procedure succeeds 95% of the time in the long run.

title: Appendix A — Datasets
text:
This appendix will catalog all datasets used in the textbook with descriptions, sources, and download links.

Datasets used in this textbook are drawn primarily from:

The openintro R package (400+ datasets)
The IMS dataset collection
Public sources (Data.gov, UCI Machine Learning Repository)
Local and regional datasets from the University of Wisconsin-La Crosse

All datasets are available in CSV format for use with any statistical software.
